## Why emulate a simulator?

- An ODE solve can be accurate but too expensive inside calibration, uncertainty
  analysis, or design.
- A surrogate approximates a declared simulator response on a declared domain.
- The mechanistic model remains the arbiter for decisions.

::: {.notes}
Emphasize that a surrogate is a computational approximation, not a new causal
model. The held-out error plot is more important than the training fit.
:::

## A small, explicit target

Classification: deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population-level.

$$
\dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\quad
\dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\quad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

For $\beta\in[0.02,0.08]$, emulate

$$
q(\beta)=R(40;\beta)/N,\qquad
e_j=\widehat q(\beta_j)-q(\beta_j).
$$

Baseline: $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$, $N=1000$, $c=10$, $\gamma=0.25$.

## Design, simulate, fit

```{julia}
using CairoMakie, EpiModelingCourse, OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random, Statistics, Surrogates

function q(β)
    p = SIRParameters(beta=β, contact_rate=10.0, gamma=0.25, N=1000.0)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), p),
                Tsit5(); saveat=[40.0], abstol=1e-9, reltol=1e-9)
    sol[3, end] / p.N
end

Random.seed!(20260711)
lb, ub = 0.02, 0.08
β_train = sample(12, lb, ub, LatinHypercubeSample())
y_train = q.(β_train)
emulator = RadialBasis(β_train, y_train, lb, ub; rad=cubicRadial())
```

::: {.notes}
The Latin-hypercube design is small so the approximation error is large enough
to see and the example stays quick to run. `RadialBasis` is callable in
Surrogates.jl 7; `cubicRadial()` is the current constructor form.
:::

## The diagnostic is out of sample

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Mechanistic SIR output, radial-basis surrogate, training design, and held-out approximation error."
β_grid = collect(range(lb, ub; length=64))
y_true, y_hat = q.(β_grid), emulator.(β_grid)
errors = y_hat .- y_true

fig = Figure(size=(850, 350))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel="β", ylabel="R(40) / N")
lines!(ax1, β_grid, y_true, label="SIR")
lines!(ax1, β_grid, y_hat, label="surrogate")
scatter!(ax1, β_train, y_train, label="training")
axislegend(ax1)
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel="β", ylabel="absolute error")
scatter!(ax2, β_grid, abs.(errors))
fig
```

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{m^{-1}\sum_j e_j^2}.
$$

## Validate, then use

- Check the emulator on held-out inputs, not only training points.
- Refine locally with `Surrogates.update!` when error identifies a gap.
- For two or more inputs, scale the design and increase training points.
- Re-simulate every policy or scientific conclusion with the original model.

```{julia}
Surrogates.update!(emulator, 0.051, q(0.051))
(rmse=sqrt(mean(errors.^2)), max_abs_error=maximum(abs.(errors)))
```

## Limits and links

- Extrapolation outside the design interval is not validated.
- A peak or threshold target can need many more points than a smooth final size.
- Solver failures and observation noise must be represented in the training
  pipeline rather than hidden in one scalar response.

See the [book appendix](../../appendices/07-surrogate-models.html), the
[Surrogates radial-basis docs](https://docs.sciml.ai/Surrogates/stable/radials/),
and the [surrogate interface](https://docs.sciml.ai/Surrogates/stable/surrogate/).

::: {.notes}
Takeaway: design, fit, validate, and retain the simulator. A low RMSE is a
local statement about this target, domain, and numerical implementation.
:::
